chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Disc jockeys Fred Robbins and Symphony Sid, and jazz parasites
summary: Wilson laments Robbins interviewing movie stars and recalls Symphony Sid failing to recognize Tatum, calling hangers-on parasites.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: hear Fred Robins with the American Armed Forces doing a stupid thing called The Sign of Hollywood. Today he was interviewing Paul McCartney -- how does it feel when you hear a Beatles record?

Fred Robins, who used to be the greatest jazz jockey in America, he's working overseas with that stuff, and I hear him all the time, he's interviewing movie stars, the most nobody people, and asking them the most stupid questions like you would see in Screen Love magazine or something. Fred Robins, the best disc jockey that this country ever had, to me, when he was down in New York. I mean, the boys wrote Robin's Nest and dedicated it to him, Jacquet and Charlie Thompson.

And here he is asking Paul McCartney, well, how do you feel when you hear a Beatles record? You know, that's one of the stupid questions they ask when you wonder what are they supposed to say? What is he supposed to feel? Hey, here's a Beatle record, yeah! All right.
I just hate to see that, every time they bring Fred on, it really brings me down.

Because, see, I hate to see guys like him abandon jazz, like Symphony Sid, I knew he had no principles at all, you know, he was at a party once at Billy Eckstine's apartment and Ted's mother was there, and they put an

Art Tatum record on the thing, and he didn't know who the piano player was. And in those days, nobody sounded like Art Tatum. Nobody remotely. And he was the top, head man of the be bop movement, Symphony Sid, the hippest jazz jock -- and he didn't know who the piano player was.
You know, I told you that last night.

So these people, these parasites who are alongside of these creative jazz players, they don't help them. They suck what money they can get out of them and the only ones who really help are people like John Hammond, because he came in with the money, and the others who have taken less money out, but have done some good. Like you have to give credit to George Wein and Norman Granz, because they have not been negative; they made money, but again, their people have made money, too.
